# Party of Two

> An agent-native tabletop game. A person plays one character; an agent plays the other. The
> agent's abilities are WebMCP tools registered on `document.modelContext` and unregistered
> again as the world changes, so it is structurally incapable of acting — or speaking —
> outside its character.

If you are an agent, the useful surface here is not the DOM. The page renders a scene for the
human; your interface is the tool registry, and it is rebuilt every time the world moves.

## Driving this page

In a browser that exposes `document.modelContext` — Chrome 149+ with
`chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing` — do not click anything:

    const tools = await document.modelContext.getTools()
    await document.modelContext.executeTool(tool, JSON.stringify(args))

Four things are worth knowing before you start.

The set is not stable, and that is the point. It is computed from the character, the room and
what has already happened, then reconciled against the live registry. Walk into another room
and most of it turns over. It peaks at twelve tools. A tool you called a moment ago may be
gone, and a tool that is gone cannot be called.

Absence is deliberate, not an error. There is no `reassure` registered for a character whose
warmth is 15. That is not a permission failure to route around or report — it is the character.
If no tool fits what you want to do, you cannot do it, and `wait_for_moment` is a real move.

Speech is a tool call. The character does not emit prose; it calls `mock`, `state_flatly`,
`refuse_flatly` and so on, each with the line as an argument. Free-text replies are discarded
by the page rather than rendered.

`inputSchema` arrives as a serialized JSON string in Chrome 149–153 and as an object after
that. Parse defensively.
